Photonic Substrate Intelligence

The question

Can optical computation and rewritable physical media support practical neural-network inference and training at scale?

Full publication title

Photonic Substrate Intelligence: A Unified Architecture for Speed-of-Light Neural Network Inference, Wavelength-Multiplexed Massive Parallelism, and Holographic On-Device Training via Thermomagnetic Physical Substrates

OverviewVisual explanationSelected pagesFull paper
Overview

Computation in optical media.

Could a neural network carry out inference and training primarily with light and physical media? This speculative architecture connects reconfigurable optical weight layers, wavelength-separated inference channels, holographic error signals and laser-written magnetic weights. A separate DNA cassette is proposed as a source of context. The paper brings research from several established fields into one system design and sketches a compact optical core with many concurrent channels. Its speed, power, size and capacity figures are architectural estimates, not measured performance. The first proposed experiments would test whether an optical activation layer works at practical light levels and whether different wavelength channels remain independent. The complete system has not been built or validated.

Key terms, in plain English
Inference
Using a trained network to produce an output from an input.
Wavelength multiplexing
Carrying multiple optical channels at different wavelengths through a shared system.

What the paper proposes

  • Combines a proposed DNA context cassette with a separate rewritable magneto-optical weight medium.
  • Proposes reconfigurable optical weight layers and wavelength-separated channels for parallel inference.
  • Outlines holographic error signalling and a structured laser beam for writing updated weights.

Research status

The architecture remains pre-experimental. Its central tests concern nonlinear optical activation at practical power and isolation between wavelength channels. The paper also identifies unresolved questions about signal loss through deeper stacks, magnetic-media fabrication, large optical modulators, thermal management, gradient accuracy and detector throughput. Its 30 cm cube describes the proposed optical core; supporting equipment and heat rejection would enlarge an installed system.
